ARCHIVES COMMITTEE 

The activities of this Committee were concentrated on the Interna¬ 
tional Congress held in Toronto, January 26-29. Prior to this event, 
requests went to the Provincial Associations for slide trays depicting 
camp scenes representative of that province. The following Provin¬ 
cial Associations brought slide carousels and slides which were 
shown in the Archives Room. 

Newfoundland, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Ontario, 
Saskatchewan and Nova Scotia. 

Due to the efforts of a large number of people, but notably Helen 
Stewart, Bernadine Dodge and Ken Johnston, the Archives Room 
contained a splendid display of archival material enriched by exhibits 
from the Kanawa Museum provided by Professor Kirk Wipper and 
assisted by Eanswyth Flynn. In addition to the many pictorial dis¬ 
plays, a photographic record of all former CCA Presidents was 
prepared consisting of two frames with empty spaces for the next 
five CCA Presidents. 

The official opening of the Archives Room was attended by a large 
number of delegates from various parts of Canada. While wine and 
cheese was being enjoyed, the Chairman made a strong plea to 
those present to keep in mind that the records of today are the 
archives of tomorrow. He urged them to send all materials relating to 
the business of the Provincial Association to the CCA office for 
deposit at Trent University. The Chairman also expressed the hope 
that every Provincial Association will keep one of its members 
designated as the Archives Chairman whose job it will be to keep the 
CCA Committee informed. 

It would take too long to mention the many volunteers who have 
so greatly contributed to the work of the Archives Committee but 
special mention must be made of Marjorie Booth and Helen Stewart 
who gave unstintingly of their time and talents. 

Finally, your Chairman will be expecting a steady stream of 
communication from the various Provincial Associations. 

Bruno Morawetz, Ph.D. 


EDUCATION COMMITTEE 

The action plan for this committee included a workshop to be held as 
a pre-congress event in January 1983. This goal was reached and 
the objectives for the workshop were achieved. 

On January 25, 25, sixteen delegates representing every prov¬ 
ince met in Toronto with the three members of the Education 
Committee to discuss the proposed curriculum which forms the 
basis for the professional development of camp directors. The 
method used during the first day was to assign small discussion 
groups the topics of the curriculum. Each report to the total group on 
acceptance or changes suggested by the group was then ratified and 
by the end of the first day, all topics had been reviewed and ratified. 

On the second day of the workshop, the groups re-formed to 
discuss the recommended methods for delivery for each specific 
topic. After lunch, discussions, by province, focussed on the ways in 
which the province could make this curriculum available to its 
members; and where they might require additional resources to 
accomplish this goal. 

The final section of the workshop concentrated on the recom¬ 
mendations to the Education Committee and to the Canadian 
Camping Association for future action. These recommendations will 
form the basis of the Education Committee’s work for the next year; 
and will be specifically set out in the workshop report to the Presi¬ 
dent. As chairman, the dedication to the task by the delegates; and 


the support of John Wilkinson and Stan Talesnick as committee 
members and resource persons for the two days was sincerely 
appreciated. 

Dorothy Walter 

ENVIRONMENT COMMITTEE 

No report submitted. 


EXECUTIVE WORKSHOP 
TASK FORCE 

As a newly appointed chairman of the Executive Workshop, I can 
only report on the brief exercise I’ve performed and the plan for ’83 
that will coincide with G. Ivan Robinson’s report last year and the 
Action Plan Objective in May of 1981 being: “to conduct by 1983 a 
pilot project of an annual workshop for volunteer executive mem¬ 
bers serving in Provincial Association which will focus on volun- 
teerism”. 

Ivan had circulated a questionnaire to the provincial association 
presidents and CCA executive members in 1982. The results were 
summarized and the following is a summary: 


MOST IMPORTANT 


LEAST IMPORTANT 


1. Short term Association planning. 

2. Assessment of needs of those for 
whom they are responsible. 

2. Coping with Association 
demands/responsibilities. 

3. Decision making (consensus, 
leading meetings, decisions, 
application etc.). 

4. Organizational development - 
transitions, orientation, progressions 
etc. 

5. Problem solving. 

6. Fundraising. 

6. Budget formulation and 
management. 

7. Administrative procedures. 

8. Relationship with 
governments/Provincial, Federal. 

9. Conducting effective meetings. 

10. Policy formulation and 

implementation. 


The CCA board has established October 12-16, 1983 in the 
Toronto area to be the time and place where this pilot project will first 
happen. It must be noted that confirmation of this event will be made 
only if Fitness Canada approves the submission to provide airfares 
for participants. 

As a result of a small group of CCA board members who helped to 
summarize the results of the questionnaire, the following will be the 
focus of the 1983 Executive Workshop: 

1. Boardmanship Training - facilitation, training, consultation, etc. 

2. Board level skills - problem analysis, decision making, how to be 
accountable etc. 

3. Financial responsibilities - fund raising, responsible decision 
making, accountability etc. 

4. Board Task Development - leadership, effective committee 
work, group consensus, how to lead a meeting, taking of min¬ 
utes, log recommendations etc. 


5. Future Boardmanship Stimulation - beyond survival, National 
and Provincial issues, futures, environment, economy, energy, 
staff development. 

The Workshop will be for: 

a) CCA/ACC Board members and will provide provincial repre¬ 
sentatives with a model that can be used in their home provinces. 

b) And one other provincial representative with potential as a Board 
member. 

Mr. Arnie Cohen, Winnipeg, MB has consented to serve as 
resource person. Arnie is presently writing a book on volunteerism 
as a board member of non-profit organizations. 

£ 

Terry Burkhalter 


IMMIGRATION TASK FORCE 

The protocol worked out between the Federal Ministry of Employ¬ 
ment and Immigration and the writer, together with the Executive 
Director, during our meeting in Ottawa, has continued to serve well 
the needs of Canadian camps wishing to employ some foreign camp 
counsellors. Year by year these procedures are becoming used and 
accepted by camps across Canada, making the hiring of foreign 
camp counsellors a smooth operation. We appreciate the continuing 
support and co-operation we have received from the federal offi¬ 
cials. Whenever a problem has arisen, they have been quick to help. 

Few problems occurred during 1982, when they did arise they 
were due to camps not following the protocol step by step. 

We have given three undertakings to the Federal Ministry: 

1. That camps will endeavour to follow faithfully the steps as set out 
in the protocol. 

2. That every effort will be made to hire a “Canadian” before 
requesting permission to employ a foreign camp counsellor. 

3. That camps will provide basic statistical information to their 
provincial associations, which will be collated by the Canadian 
Camping office and forwarded to this Ministry. 

This statistical information is confidential and anonymous and 
imperative if we are to continue to justify our requests. 

We urge you to provide the statistical information requested. 

The statistics compiled by the Federal Government are in the 
chart which follows. 

Barry Lowes 


CONSULTATION/SPEAKERS 
BUREAU TASK FORCE 

The objective of the Consultation Speakers Bureau was to develop a 
list of National Consultant/Speakers who could be called upon to 
address various topics related to camping. This list was then to be 
circulated to provinces and to be used for various Conferences and 
Workshops. 

The Task Force in reviewing Conference Brochures, and work¬ 
shop Speakers realized that it was very difficult to come up with a 
definitive list of speakers for any particular topic. Also, with people 
moving and changing job positions, they were not always available 
as they were at the time of being listed. 

As a result, the difficulty of compiling a list and keeping it updated, 
and recognizing that provinces who are running workshops and 
conferences will contact persons that they know, I am recommend¬ 
ing that the Consultants/Speakers Bureau Task Force be either 
incorporated with the Consultants Advisors Project, or that it be 
dropped as a Task Force of the Canadian Camping Association. 

Wayne Perkins 


FRENCH LANGUAGE COMMITTEE 

The chairman’s position was vacant for several months this year. We 
were, therefore, pleased to confirm Pauline Rondeau as Chairman 
in March 1983. 

During the past year, the Editor of “CANADIAN CAMPING” has 
produced the editorial in both French and English. 

The other major achievement this year was the provision of 
simultaneous interpretation of all key-note speakers at the Con¬ 
gress, in addition to three French sessions offered to francophone 
delegates. The bilingual text provided in the promotional literature 
and program of the Congress also reflected the effort to include both 
language groups. 

Next year we hope to attract articles in French for the inclusion in 
“CANADIAN CAMPING”. Further, we plan to establish translation 
priorities and procedures so that all CCA/ACC volunteers know 
what, when and how translation should be done. 

Jane McCutcheon

INTERNATIONAL CAMPING 
CONGRESS/ TASKFORCE 

The International Camping Congress is now history - but what an 
experience it was for over 1,000 delegates. We had speakers and 
delegates from Canada, U.S.A., Norway, Japan, Great Britain, 
Jamaica, Mexico, Australia and New Zealand. After four years of 
hard work, the Steering Committee was gratified to see that its faith 
in this project was justified. 

Special thanks should go to all the 60 volunteers who worked on 
the organizing committees, all the provincial presidents who helped 
promote the Congress and recruited speakers and delegates, the 
hundreds of donors and to the OCA and CCA/ACC staff, to Fitness 
Canada and the Government of Ontario, all of whom contributed so 
much to our success. 

This Congress was a remarkable achievement. The results of the 
Congress can already be seen across Canada in the leadership and 
activity levels of the provincial associations. It proves once again the 
truth of our Congress theme: TOGETHER WE ARE STRONGER. 

John Latimer 


LEADERSHIP DEVELOPMENT 
PROGRAM COMMITTEE 

Under the Consultant/Advisor project funded by Fitness Canada 
during 1982-83, the chart below outlines the resource people spon¬ 
sored and the respective costs. The CCA/ACC appreciates the 
learning opportunities made possible through this Fitness Canada 
grant. Each participant returns to his/her camp to train other camp 
leaders in the new activity skills which will be passed along to 
hundreds of campers. 

Two subsequent C/A requests from B.C. for Jack Pearse and 
Manitoba for Jay Haddad have been approved by the national 
executive for internal funding. The wide use of this project to train 
provincial leaders in various skill areas for camps is evident. It was, 
therefore, disappointing to learn that Fitness Canada did not ap¬ 
prove funding to carry on the Consultant/Advisor program for 
1983-84.

1985 NATIONAL CONFERENCE 
TASKFORCE 

The Task Force realized that it would be logical to study the feasibility 
of any National Conference in 1985 after the results of the Interna¬ 
tional Camping Congress were known. As a result, a questionnaire 
was circulated to the provinces in March. The provincial responses 
will be available in May so the Task Force will complete its recom¬ 
mendations soon after. 

Jack Pearse 

NEWSLETTER COMMITTEE 

“CANADIAN CAMPING” has had a big year! We completed our 
first volume using the format established in 1981-82. The response 
to the newsletter was certainly gratifying if not overwhelming. 

Two new features became regular additions in the newsletter: the 
winning photograph and the camp advisor column. 

Several articles were submitted from many provinces. My sincere 
thanks to those members who contributed articles, poems, recipes 
and photographs last year. As a result, we were able to expand the 
newsletter to twenty pages. However, we still need coast-to-coast 
content so all members should try to get involved! 

Next year we plan to increase the advertising and subscription 
revenue so that we can continue to improve CANADIAN CAMP¬ 
ING. 

Jay Haddad 

NOMINATIONS COMMITTEE 

By January 31, 1983, there was only one nomination received for 
each elected office on the CCA/ACC Executive. Therefore the 
following persons have been elected by acclamation: 

President Jocelyn Palm (Ontario) 

Eastern Vice President George Matthews (Nova Scotia) 

Central Vice President Louis Jean (Quebec) 

Western Vice President Terry Burkhalter (Manitoba) 

These persons will serve for a two year term commencing with the 
CCA/ACC Annual Meeting on May 6, 1983. 

Congratulations to all the new Executive Officers for 1983-1985. 
Cliff Labbett 

PUBLICITY & PUBLIC RELATIONS 

I have been really fortunate this year to meet many Directors and 
camp staff across the country. Through the auspices of CCA, 
personal travel, and the International Congress, I have visited 
Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Alberta and Ontario and attended meet¬ 
ings and conferences there. Getting to know the people and the 
camps which make up CCA is an essential part of promotion, and I 
want to thank everyone for being so kind and welcoming. 

The major work I have done this year, obviously, revolves around 
the launching of National Camping Day. First there was the prepara¬ 
tion and giving of the Pre-Congress Workshop on Promotions in 
Toronto, January 25 and 26. This was a really good gathering - 
allowing interchange, discussion and education. The provincial 
delegates had an opportunity to broaden their knowledge of camp¬ 
ing in Canada, as well as of PR. I wish to thank the provincial 
organizations for selecting such good delegates, who came to share 
and to learn, and to those delegates themselves, who gave of their 
time to attend the workshop, and to work for CCA. 

Since the workshop, hours have been spent on getting the posters 
designed, printed, and mailed; on mailings; communications; pro¬ 
vincial events, etc. Not only my time, but that of each delegate and a 
lot of effort by Jocelyn Palm and Marjorie Booth has gone in to 


making National Camping Day happen. 

An article has been prepared for the CCA publication, and 
something will appear in all future issues. The next three National 
Camping Days are already in the works, so we look for bigger and 
better things each year. 

This report, of necessity, is written before April 14 - look for 
specific results and a report in the next magazine. At this point, 
however, I can say that things look good. At the Pre-Congress 
Workshop, the New Brunswick delegates used the words “baby 
steps” to talk about their beginnings into PR. Well, we have taken 
those baby steps as a national association this year. Some will say 
they are too small, some say too big. However, you must take them 
before you can walk, and then run, and I think we have made secure 
baby steps. 6,500 posters have been distributed across the country 
to member camps. Delay in the distribution was unfortunate, and I 
apologize, but one learns from all experiences and the 1984 posters 
will be out by January 1. A special public thanks goes to Peter 
Goddard and the staff of Kamp Kanawana in Montreal for accepting 
the tremendous task of mailing to every camp. 

Two Press Releases have been written and distributed to the 
national media - including 600 weekly newspapers. A CCA fact 
sheet and copy of the artwork were included with these. Three Press 
Releases have been written and distributed through the provincial 
delegates. Nova Scotia and New Brunswick have both had the Day 
declared by the Ministers involved and Saskatchewan has applied 
for that too. New Brunswick, in fact, has an entire camping week, as 
does Quebec. In Ontario, the Society of Camp Directors will meet 
on April 14 to celebrate, and in Alberta some of the posters are being 
distributed through the school system and a team of speakers has 
been lined up. In B.C., they hope to tie the visit of their Consultant/ 
Advisor, Jack Pearse, in to their radio and TV coverage. Manitoba is 
using local newspapers and radio stations to spread the word, as well 
as camper notices and church announcements. Saskatchewan 
hopes to tie in the promotion of NCD with that of their Conference, 
by using radio and print media announcements. 

Both Nova Scotia and New Brunswick have distributed the Press 
Releases to all camps, and N.S. is getting the support of the 
Minister’s office to do the media work. I think these are good first 
steps, and all involved are to be congratulated. As a volunteer 
organization, one can only expect so much from each person and 
this is a tremendous undertaking. Thanks should go to each dele¬ 
gate for their work and time, on your behalf. 

Here’s to March 21, 1984 - the 2nd Annual National Camping 
Day. We’ve been through the ropes once; we’ve learned a great deal 
and we have a good national team. I am sure it will be an even bigger 
success than this one. 

A special note of appreciation goes to Gary Luthy and Jane 
McCutcheon, two Vice-Presidents who are stepping down this year. 
Both have been personal supporters since I took on this role, and 
have helped create National Camping Day. I’ll miss them. 

I have been keeping in touch with the Pre-Congress delegates, the 
Provincial Presidents, and the CCA Executive since January. They 
are well informed on all aspects of the project, so if you have any 
specific questions, or wish to lend your talents, please contact 
someone from your province. I want to thank all of these people for 
putting up with me, for reading the scads of paper I send, and for 
their encouragement and support. National Camping Day is the 
biggest national project CCA has ever undertaken. It’s been a great 
deal of work, but I feel fortunate indeed to have been in on the birth 
of such a promising event, and for having had the opportunity to 
have met and worked with so many special people. 

Marnie M. Ellis 


PUBLICATIONS COMMITTEE 

The Publications Committee is pleased to report that Legacy to a 
Camper - the story of Mary S. Edgar by Jocelyn Palm is printed and 
available to the public. Jocelyn has donated Legacy to the CCA and 
all proceeds from the book go to the association. Many may have 
already secured a copy at the Congress or through the CCA Publica¬ 
tions Service. 

An editorial committee is preparing the final draft of the CIT 
Manual scheduled for release by May 1, 1983. This practical guide 
designed for use in counsellor-in-training programs will feature 
instructor insert notes. 

The Publications Committee has elected to change the name of 
the Publications Service to the CCA Bookstore, effective September 
1983. 

We have made an effort to increase revenues at conferences by 
sending some titles in bulk as well as having catalogues available. At 
the International Camping Congress we had the use of three exhibit 
spaces. We tried to increase sales by an author signing event, a 
special sale table, notices in the Congress newspaper and the new 
CCA bookmark promoting the “How To” Series. 

We realize the potential of the CCA Publications to raise funds to 
support other CCA Activities, therefore our major objectives for 
1983-84 is to actively seek new opportunities to sell CCA’s own 
publications. 

Finally, we would like to thank Gary Luthy for his assistance as our 
liaison with the CCA Executive and Board. 

Beth Moon, Wendy Wren, Judy Richards

This project went into operation with the printing of 500 packages of

hasti notes. Seventy-six packages have been sold as of March 1983. 
They will be advertised in the next issue of Canadian Camping and 
be available at publication displays at various conferences. 

Further items will be developed as 1983 progresses. 

Janet Adamson 

STANDARDS TASK FORCE 

The major role of the Standards Task Force this year was to plan and 
operate the National Standards Workshop in Toronto, January 
25-26, 1983. 

Our objectives were two-fold: 

• update the existing comparative analysis of provincial standards 
for organized camping 

• review and document extensively the visitation process vis a vis 
the education component for camps (personal and boards), pro¬ 
vincial governments (legislation affecting camps) and funding 
bodies 

The delegates worked diligently before the Workshop to have the 
provincial comparisons ready so that our time together would be 
most beneficial. 

The Workshop has proposed that CCA/ACC should not accredit 
camps but should promote good camping practices through educa¬ 
tion of camp directors. This, of course, has important implications 
for our future action plan and for provincial camping associations. 
Therefore, we have asked the National Board of Directors to con¬ 
tinue the Standards Task Force review for 18 months and convene 
another National Workshop in 1985 to resolve the need for a 
Standing Committee on Standards. 

Brian Law

Canada’s forests are in crisis and the future 
depends on dynamic action by all Canadians, 
young and old, participating in public aware¬ 
ness, education, tree planting and conserva¬ 
tion. 

The United Nations, concerned that prati- 
cally all nations are cutting trees faster than 
they are being planted, has initiated a world¬ 
wide tree planting program with the slogan 
“FOR EVERY CHILD ATREE”. 

The Canadian Foundation for World Devel¬ 
opment launched a nationwide campaign to 
motivate every Canadian to plant trees to pre¬ 
serve our heritage of forests and implement 
conservation measures. The enthusiastic re¬ 
sponse from governments at all levels, indus¬ 
tries, educational institutions, religious 
groups, unions, service organizations and in¬ 
dividuals, clearly indicates that there is a gen¬ 
uine concern and a positive motivation to be 
involved. This program supports and comple¬ 
ments all those organizations who now carry 
out effective programs. 

Special thanks is due the Ottawa Board of 
Education for its enthusiastic initiative with a 
plan to involve each of its 54 elementary 


schools in planting 100 trees and each of its 24 
secondary schools in planting 200 trees. 
Every School Board across Canada is chal¬ 
lenged to develop similar creative programs. 
Already several have announced their pro¬ 
grams. Interesting suggestions include plant¬ 
ing trees along highways and municipal 
roads; at cloverleafs; along freeways; in val¬ 
leys, towns and cities. 

In Ontario trees are provided free to schools 
for educational purposes and are available 
through their nearest Ministry of Natural Re¬ 
sources Office. Individual schools or boards 
are requested to submit a project outline with 
their tree application and written approval of 
the owner of the property. Most native Ontario 
tree species of commercial importance are 
available. 

Canadian camps can participate in “For 
Every Child A Tree” with innovative involve¬ 
ment such as planting a tree recognizing 
birthdays, memorials and special occasions. 
Posters and educational materials are avail¬ 
able. 

This is your special invitation to be an ac¬ 
tive participant in this nationwide “Tree Pro¬ 
gram”. It is an on-going program that 
hopefully will achieve a significant profile by 
1985 “The International Year of Youth”. It is 
hoped that a Canadian United Nations Youth 
Parliament can be developed thereby helping 
us to become more sensitive to the needs of 
Third World Countries and the interdepen¬ 
dence of all nations. 

For further information please contact... 
The Canadian Foundation for 
World Development 
2441 Bay view Avenue 
Willowdale, Ontario 
M2L1A5 
416-445-4740

INTERNATIONAL YOUTH YEAR 
LOGO CONTEST 

The Canadian Camping Association, International 
Youth Year Task Force invites all campers and staff to 
assist in the designing of a logo for the 1985 International 
Youth Year. 

Encourage your campers and staff to participate in the 
event to launch CCA activities for 1985. 

Contest Rules - 

(A) Logo must depict camping and youth 

(B) Logo submissions shall measure 5” x 5” (12.7 cm x 
12.7 cm) 

(C) Maximum of 2 colors allowed in logo including 
background color 

(D) All wording shall be bilingual 

Deadline for submissions - all entries should be for¬ 
warded to: 

Canadian Camping Association 
1806 Avenue Road 
Suite 2 

Toronto, Ontario 
M5M 3Z1 

Entries must be received at the CCA office by Septem¬ 
ber 15,1983. 

PRIZES - Appropriate prizes will be awarded to the top 
three entries in the contest. 

All entries shall become the property of the Canadian 
Camping Association and will not be returned.

articles and much, much more.. .your staff will thank you, your campers will benefit!
